items.text: ACID-BASEINDICATORS

items.label: text
items.text: Earlierinthissectionwelooked atthepHtitrationcurves obtained when an aqueous solution of an acid is added to an aqueoussolutionofabase.Thefourcasesweconsideredwere:

items.label: list_item
items.text: ·strong acid-strongbase

items.label: list_item
items.text: weak acid-strongbase

items.label: list_item
items.text: strong acid-weak base

items.label: list_item
items.text: weakacid-weakbase.

items.label: text
items.text: We are now going to use these four curves to help us understand why different indicators arerequiredfor different types of titrations.

items.label: text
items.text: An acid-base indicatoris either aweak acid or a weak base. Mostindicators areweak acids(HIn).Foran indicator that is a weak acid, its dissociation in aqueous solution can be represented as:

items.label: text
items.text: HIn(aq) = H+(aq) + In-(aq)

items.label: text
items.text: The molecule, HIn, and its conjugate base, In, have different colours in aqueous solution.For methyl orange, these are red and yellow,respectively:

items.label: formula
items.text:
HIn(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + In⁻(aq)
red                       yellow

items.label: text
items.text: When [H+(aq)] is sufficiently large the equilibrium will shift far enough to the left for the red colour to predominate. If [H+(aq)] is verylowthentheequilibriumwillliefarovertotherightandthe yellow colour will predominate.Therefore,the indicator changes colour accordingtothepHofthesolution.
